opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the biggest thing they miss is that most benchmarks are fairly static snapshots. You give the model a question, it gives you an answer, and you score it. But a huge part of human cognition is what happens over time: learning something new on the fly, holding onto it, and building on it later.

Take episodic memory. If you go to a new job, in the first week you're picking up a lot of specific details: who does what, where things are, what went wrong last Tuesday. You remember these things quickly, sometimes after a single exposure, and they shape how you act from then on. Current models don't really have that. They have what's in the weights, which is learned slowly over enormous amounts of data, and they have what's in the context window, which is a kind of working memory. But that middle layer, rapidly forming durable memories of specific experiences and integrating them, is largely missing. And our benchmarks mostly don't test for it, because they're not designed around an agent that accumulates experience.

Another thing is that we tend to test the things that are easy to test. Language, math, coding, knowledge questions. Those matter, but human cognition is much broader. There's a whole set of capabilities we take for granted because even a child has them: understanding a physical environment, keeping track of objects, planning over long horizons, noticing that something you just did didn't work and adjusting. Models can look superhuman on a benchmark and then fail at things that would be trivial for an ordinary person.

So my view has been that to really know whether you've reached something like human-level general intelligence, you can't rely on any single benchmark. You need a broad battery of the cognitive tasks typical humans can do. And then, importantly, you need people actively trying to find things a typical human can do that the system can't. When it becomes really hard to find those failure cases, that's when I'd be fairly confident we've gotten there. We're not quite at that point yet, but the list of gaps is getting shorter.

r001.rationale: It identifies episodic memory as rapidly learning and retaining specific experiences, and says benchmarks mostly do not test this.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes the context window as a kind of working memory.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes context-window working memory from missing episodic memory, but does not say that increasing context windows is an attempt to compensate for that gap.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that benchmarks are very good at measuring the things that are easy to measure, and that's not an accident. You write down a question, you have a reference answer, you score it. And so the whole field drifts toward capabilities that fit that format: recall, pattern completion, short-horizon reasoning where the answer is checkable in a sentence or two.

But if you look at what humans actually do with their intelligence, a huge fraction of it isn't like that at all. It's extended over time. You're pursuing some goal over hours, days, months. You're building up a model of a situation, noticing when your model is wrong, revising it, and carrying that forward. The memory isn't a context window that gets wiped, it's cumulative. You come back the next day and you still know what you learned. Most benchmarks test a system in a single shot, so they say almost nothing about whether it can learn continually from experience in the way even a child does.

The second thing is what I'd call the breadth of the distribution. When I think about general intelligence, and this goes back to work Marcus Hutter and I did many years ago, the key idea is performance across a very wide range of environments, including ones you haven't seen before. A benchmark is, by construction, a fixed distribution. Once it exists, it's in the training data, or something very like it is, and so you end up measuring how well the system has absorbed that particular distribution rather than how well it would do on something genuinely novel. Humans are quite good at being dropped into a new game, a new culture, a new tool, and figuring it out with a handful of examples. Our models are getting better at that, but the benchmarks don't really isolate it.

The third thing, which I think is underrated, is the very ordinary stuff. Humans have an enormous amount of embodied, physical, social common sense that we never consciously think about. Knowing that if you knock a glass off a table it'll break, knowing that someone who's gone quiet in a meeting might be upset, knowing roughly how long it takes to walk across the room. Models are now often superhuman on graduate-level exam questions while still occasionally failing things a ten-year-old finds trivial. That jagged profile is one of the most interesting facts about these systems, and a single aggregate score completely hides it.

So when people ask me, are we at AGI yet, my answer has always been that I want to see a system that can do essentially all the cognitive things a typical person can do, not just the ones that happen to be easy to write exams for. And I think the honest position is that our benchmarks are a lagging indicator of what matters, and we need to be putting much more effort into measuring the long-horizon, open-ended, learning-from-experience side of things.

r001.rationale: The response discusses cumulative learning from experience but does not identify rapid learning of specific experiences through episodic memory.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a wiped context window with cumulative memory, but does not compare context windows to human working memory.

r003.rationale: It does not describe expanding context windows as an attempt to compensate for a lack of episodic memory.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the big things is learning as you go. With most benchmarks, you train a model, freeze it, and then ask it a collection of questions. That tells you something useful about its capabilities, but it doesn’t really tell you how well it can enter an unfamiliar situation, work out what’s going on, and acquire a new skill through experience.

If you look at a human starting a new job, they don’t necessarily know how to do it on day one. They ask questions, try things, get feedback, and gradually build an understanding of how that particular environment works. The interesting question is how quickly they learn, and whether what they learn helps them deal with the next problem.

I’d like to see more evaluations of that process. Put the system in an environment where it has something genuinely new to learn, give it time to interact, and measure its progress. Can it identify what it doesn’t understand? Can it choose useful experiments? Can it recover from a mistaken assumption? Those seem like important aspects of intelligence that a score on a fixed set of questions only captures indirectly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning through experience but does not identify episodic memory or rapid learning of specific experiences as the capability benchmarks miss.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison between model context windows and human working memory.

r003.rationale: It does not mention increasing context windows or frame them as compensation for lacking episodic memory.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest things they miss is the ability to learn something genuinely new. With a human, you can introduce an unfamiliar task, explain a few things, let them experiment, and watch how their understanding develops. Most benchmarks give you a snapshot: here’s a question, can you produce the right answer? That’s useful, but it doesn’t tell you very much about the process of acquiring a capability.

And with language models, there’s this difficulty of knowing how novel the task really is. Has the model encountered something very similar during training? You can change the wording, but that doesn’t necessarily change the underlying problem.

What I’d like to see more of is an evaluation where the system enters an unfamiliar environment, has to work out what matters, and improves through experience. Can it form a hypothesis, test it, notice that it’s wrong, and change its approach? Can it carry what it learned into a different situation? I think that would tell us something about intelligence that a collection of static exam questions doesn’t capture.
